summary: Defines MIB objects for managing optical interfaces associated with wavelength division multiplexing systems or with the Optical Transport Network. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Fiber optic links carry many colors of light. This memo defines the list of things a manager can read about them from afar.

questions: what is the optical interface mib
how to monitor optical power with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for configuring and monitoring optical links: wavelengths, optical power, trace identifiers and defects.

tldr.problem: Optical Transport Network and wavelength division multiplexing equipment needed a standard way for a network manager to read its status and performance and to configure it over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB module OPT-IF-MIB plugs optical layers (OTS, OMS, OChGroup, OCh) into the existing interface tables, then adds per-layer configuration tables and 15-minute and 24-hour performance tables.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard. It does not cover optical cross-connects, and its most sensitive writable objects can interrupt traffic if SNMP is not secured.

facts.label: Interval history
facts.value: min 4, default 32, max 96 intervals of 15 minutes

today: RFC 3591 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2003. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, so it remains the definition of OPT-IF-MIB.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3591 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with SNMP. It covers optical interfaces associated with wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) systems, or characterized by the Optical Transport Network (OTN) architecture of ITU-T Recommendation G.872.

The MIB module can be used for performance monitoring, for configuration, or both. It is written in SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580), and the memo points to RFC 3410 for the overall management framework.

The OTN definitions rest on ITU-T G.872, G.709, G.798, G.874 and G.874.1. The memo also says it does not define objects for optical cross-connects. That work was left until the interface objects had consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a menu of questions you can ask a fiber-optic machine over the network, and it follows the rules phone-company engineers already wrote for optical networks.

sections.title: Optical Layers as Interfaces
sections.content:
The module reuses the MIB-II ifTable and ifStackTable (RFC 2863). Each optical layer shows up as an interface entry, and only the ifGeneralInformationGroup needs to be supported. Three interface types are used: opticalChannel (195), opticalChannelGroup (219) and opticalTransport (196).

The layers are Optical Transmission Section (OTS), Optical Multiplex Section (OMS), Optical Channel Group (OChGroup) and Optical Channel (OCh). Because OMSn and OTSn have a one to one relationship, one opticalTransport entry covers both. Each channel entry may map to m transport entries and each transport entry to n channel entries, with m and n at least 1.

For banded amplifiers, such as separate C and L band channels, the OChGroup layer lets each band have its own interface index. If an implementation does not model bands, the OChGroup layer is simply absent.

An interface can be one bidirectional object or a pair of unidirectional sink and source objects. For a pair, the RFC recommends identical ifName values to show they belong together.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a layer cake: the cable at the bottom, a bundle of colors above it, then each single color on top. Each layer gets its own name tag so the manager can ask about it separately.

sections.title: How ifTable and ifStackTable Are Used
sections.content:
The memo gives a table per layer saying how each ifTable column is filled in. For the OTS/OMS layer, ifPhysAddress is an empty octet string, ifConnectorPresent is true(1), and ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable defaults to enabled(1). For an OChGroup, ifPhysAddress holds a wavelength range such as 1350-1650 in nanometers, and for an OCh it holds a single wavelength such as 1550.

ifOperStatus is derived from the layer's defect status. An OCh interface reports lowerLayerDown(7) if its transport or OChGroup interface is down(2). Otherwise it is down(2) if the current status objects show any defect.

The ifStackTable records which interfaces are multiplexed into which. In the RFC's example, channels j and k are stacked above transport interface i, with 0 marking the top and bottom of the stack. The inverse stack table (RFC 2864) holds the same information with higher and lower layers swapped.
sections.plainLanguage: Every layer fills out a small form with the same boxes: name, speed, color, and whether it is working. A separate list says which colors ride inside which cable.

sections.title: OTN Terms, Defects and Tandem Monitoring
sections.content:
The memo summarizes terms from the ITU-T documents. The index k selects a bit rate: k=1 is about 2.5 Gbit/s, k=2 about 10 Gbit/s and k=3 about 40 Gbit/s. The OTUk layer carries an ODUk and adds forward error correction and overhead, while the ODUk carries the payload (OPUk) plus overhead for managing an optical channel.

A trail trace identifier (TTI) is an identifier placed in the overhead of a signal. The receiver compares it with an expected source identifier (SAPI) and destination identifier (DAPI). A mismatch is a TIM defect. The detection mode can be off, SAPI only, DAPI only or both.

Defect names come from G.798 and include los (loss of signal), lof (loss of frame), ais, bdi, deg, lck, oci, plm, ssf and tim.

An ODUk termination can support 0 to 6 tandem connection monitoring (TCM) levels. Levels can be nested or cascaded. In the RFC's example, TCM1 covers the end-to-end connection A1 to A2, and TCM2 is used for segment B1-B2 and again for B3-B4.
sections.plainLanguage: A trace identifier is like a name tag on a package. The receiver checks the tag against the one it expected, and shouts if they differ. Tandem monitoring lets you check one stretch of the trip as well as the whole trip.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The module is registered under transmission 133 as optIfMibModule. It splits into groups for each layer: optIfOTMn, optIfPerfMon, optIfOTSn, optIfOMSn, optIfOChGroup, optIfOCh, optIfOTUk, optIfODUk and optIfODUkT. The first, optIfOTMnTable, describes the optical transport module: its order (1 to 900 wavelengths), whether it is reduced or full functionality, supported bit rates, interface type (IrDI or IaDI), the maximum TCM levels (0 to 6, default 3) and optical reach.

The OTS, OMS, OChGroup and OCh layers each get a configuration table plus sink and source performance tables. For each direction there are current, interval, current-day and previous-day tables.

The OTUk, ODUk and ODUkT layers get configuration tables only. They cover bit rate, trace identifiers, degraded-signal thresholds, forward error correction, general communication channels (GCC0, GCC1 and GCC2), tandem connection termination points and non-intrusive monitoring. Some tables use RowStatus so a manager can create and delete rows.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is a big filing cabinet with a drawer for each layer. Each drawer holds a settings folder and, for the top layers, folders for readings taken now, over the last few minutes and over the day.

sections.title: Defect Status Objects
sections.content:
Each layer has a CurrentStatus object, a BITS value listing the defects now present. It applies to the sink side, meaning rows whose directionality is sink(1) or bidirectional(3). The bits differ by layer: OTSn has bdiP, bdiO, bdi, tim, losP, losO and los; OMSn has ssfP, ssfO, ssf, bdiP, bdiO, bdi and losP; OCh has losP, los, oci, ssfP, ssfO and ssf.

OTUk status has tim, deg, bdi, ssf, lof, ais and lom. The ODUk termination status has oci, lck, tim, deg, bdi and ssf.

Reduced-capability systems and IrDI interfaces use only a few bits. At OTSn, only los may be set. Many TTI, DAPI, SAPI and TIM objects do not apply there.

The OTUk table also has optIfOTUkSinkFECEnabled, which says whether forward error correction at the sink is on. Its default is true(1).
sections.plainLanguage: Each layer has a row of warning lights. One means the light vanished, another means the name tag is wrong, and another means the signal is getting messy. The manager can read which lights are on.

sections.title: Performance Monitoring
sections.content:
The RFC keeps performance data for the current 15-minute interval, the current 24-hour interval, N previous 15-minute intervals with 4 <= N <= 96, and one previous 24-hour interval. After an agent restart, some previous-interval data may be missing. The minimum number of intervals is 4, the default is 32 and the maximum is 96. Intervals need not line up with wall-clock time.

The optIfPerfMonIntervalTable reports seconds elapsed in the current 15-minute interval (0 to 900) and the current day (0 to 86400), the number of available intervals and the number of invalid ones.

Most layers report optical power at the input and output, with the lowest and highest values seen in the interval. Power is in units of 0.1 dBm. These values are Integer32 rather than counters or gauges, since they can rise, fall and be negative. Lower and upper threshold objects are read-write, and a Threshold Crossing Alert (TCA) should be sent when a value reaches them.

A suspected flag marks data that may be unreliable. Laser temperature and mid-stage power monitoring are deliberately not standardized, because there was no consensus. The RFC points to a proprietary MIB or the ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB (RFC 3433) for those.
sections.plainLanguage: The equipment keeps a notebook of how strong the light was, with a page for every fifteen minutes and a summary page for each day. If the light goes too low or too high, it is supposed to raise an alarm.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects (read-write and read-create) can have disruptive effects, from invalid performance data to traffic interruptions. The RFC lists the most sensitive ones, including the maximum TCM levels (optIfOTMnTcmMax), automatic power reduction control, transmitted trail trace identifiers, expected SAPI and DAPI values, TIM detection mode and consequent action, degradation thresholds, forward error correction enabling, GCC applications, TCM mode and the lock signal settings.

Even the readable objects may be sensitive, since together they describe the performance and configuration of OTN equipment. In such environments access control, and possibly encryption, applies to GET and NOTIFY as well.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC says it is RECOMMENDED to consider SNMPv3 security, and that deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals can read or change these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these dials can switch a cable off if the wrong person turns them. So the memo says to lock the control room with strong SNMP security and let only the right people in.

sections.title: Compliance Statements
sections.content:
The module defines compliance statements that spell out what an implementation must support. optIfOtnConfigCompl covers OTN configuration and requires the groups optIfOTMnGroup and optIfOTSnCommonGroup. Other groups are mandatory only when relevant, for example when the interface type is opticalTransport (196) and the directionality includes the source or sink.

optIfPreOtnPMCompl covers pre-OTN performance monitoring and requires optIfPerfMonGroup. The threshold group is mandatory if and only if TCA notifications are implemented, and then the implementation must supply the notification definitions in an enterprise MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a rule list saying which parts a maker must build. Parts needed only for some devices are marked, so a simple device is not forced to carry everything.
